newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rocks, rhetoric fly in French immigration debate.
newsitem.headline: Rocks, rhetoric fly in French immigration debate.

text.p: French deputies traded verbal assaults in parliament on Wednesday over a controversial bill to clamp down on illegal immigration after late-night street protests against the measure turned violent.

Thirty riot police were hurt -- including one who lost a finger -- and 40 protesters were detained in clashes near the National Assembly after demonstrators began throwing rocks and other projectiles on Tuesday night, police said.

The street violence, which contrasted with a large peaceful demonstration against the immigration bill on Saturday, mirrored the invective inside the chamber which forced Assembly president Philippe Seguin to call hecklers repeatedly to order.

"By undermining the rights of immigrants you are legislating against the French people themselves," opposition Socialist deputy Julien Dray told the centre-right government on the second day of the debate.
The bill "brings no effective response to the problem of illegal immigration", he charged.
"You have a poor understanding of reality," countered Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre, accusing Dray of minimizing the threat of illegal immigration.
Tuesday night's Paris violence came at the end of a peaceful march to demand the withdrawal of the bill, which police said drew 16,000 protesters while organisers claimed 30,000.
There were no figures for injuries to protesters. Five of the 40 detained remained in custody on Wednesday.

There was also violence in Toulouse, where police used tear gas to disperse demonstrators protesting against both the bill and the presence in their southern city of the number two of the far-right National Front, Bruno Megret.
Toulouse police said five police officers were injured.

Anger over the bill spread to the diplomatic front when the president of the European Parliament threatened to cancel a meeting with French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette after several top French officials including de Charette attacked the parliament for urging that the immigration bill be withdrawn.
Jose-Maria Gil-Robles said in a statement that de Charette's words were "an unacceptable judgement on the European Parliament, its role and its dignity".

He said he would not meet the minister unless he received a "clarification" of de Charette's statement, during a Wednesday morning television interview, that the European Parliament was "not yet a parliament worthy of the name".

French President Jacques Chirac, during a meeting with Gil-Robles on Tuesday, had accused the parliament of "unacceptable interference" in French affairs for adopting the motion critical of the immigration measure.

The bill, opposed by groups from artists to human rights campaigners, aims to close loopholes in tough existing laws dating from 1993 and would grant the police extended powers to track immigrants in France.
The opposition has accused the conservative government of pandering to growing numbers of National Front voters with the approach of 1998 general elections.

Parliament's legal committee has removed the bill's most fiercely contested clause, which would have required hosts to report to the police when foreign guests subject to visa requirements left their homes.
Instead, foreigners on short-term visas will be required to report their own departure to the authorities.

Opposition Socialists and Communists, largely absent when the Assembly first debated the bill in December, are trying to delay or alter the bill with a flood of amendments during the final reading. But their tactics had no chance of success since government supporters hold four-fifths of the 577 seats.
